query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Under oxidizing conditions at high temperatures, the gas environment promotes the accelerated formation and coarsening of Cr-rich (and possibly Ti-enhanced) oxide precipitates especially at grain boundaries, which reduce intergranular cohesion and lead to embrittlement and catastrophic failure. In contrast, a reducing atmosphere slows this oxide precipitation and maintains better mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with a fine, supersaturated FCC matrix containing dispersed, small precipitates from the rapid solidification process.
generation.intervention: Modulate the gas atmosphere during elevated-temperature exposure by comparing oxidizing conditions (e.g., air or high oxygen partial pressure) with reducing conditions (e.g., hydrogen-rich or inert environments).
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (approximately 950–1300 K) under prolonged exposure; atmospheres are strictly controlled to be either oxidizing or reducing.
generation.structural_mediator: The size, distribution, and coalescence of Cr-rich oxide precipitates (and possibly related intermetallic phases) along grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: In an oxidizing atmosphere, oxygen diffuses into the alloy and reacts preferentially at grain boundaries, where residual stresses and defects are highest, leading to the growth and coalescence of Cr-rich oxides. This intergranular precipitation weakens grain boundary bonds, facilitating crack initiation and propagation under mechanical load. Under a reducing atmosphere, limited oxygen availability suppresses this process, resulting in slower degradation and better retention of the alloy's ductile properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-manufactured baseline, samples exposed to oxidizing conditions will exhibit significantly larger and more continuous grain boundary oxide precipitates, reduced ductility, lower fracture toughness, and earlier onset of catastrophic failure, whereas samples in reducing environments will show minimal grain boundary oxidation and retain a more ductile mechanical response.
generation.baseline: The initial state is the additively manufactured alloy with a relatively homogeneous distribution of fine precipitates and an intact ductile FCC matrix under ambient atmospheres.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies within the elevated temperature window of 950–1300 K and relies on controlled gas atmospheres with clearly defined oxidizing versus reducing conditions.
generation.uncertainty: Although the qualitative effect of oxidizing versus reducing atmospheres on grain boundary precipitation is supported by similar observations in other HEAs, the quantitative relationship between precipitate evolution and mechanical failure thresholds in Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 remains uncertain and will require detailed calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical sets of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples. Subject one set to an oxidizing environment (e.g., air or oxygen-enriched atmosphere) and another set to a reducing environment (e.g., H2/Ar mix) at a controlled elevated temperature (e.g., 1050 K) for identical durations. Post-exposure, characterize the microstructures with SEM/TEM and XRD to quantify grain boundary precipitate size, density, and phase composition. Perform standardized tensile and fracture toughness tests to evaluate mechanical degradation.
measurements: Grain boundary precipitate size, volume fraction, and distribution using SEM/TEM imaging
Phase identification and changes using X-ray diffraction
Mechanical property measurements including tensile strength, ductility, and fracture toughness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidizing environment samples do not display a statistically significant increase in intergranular precipitate coarsening and associated degradation in mechanical properties compared to reducing environment samples, then the proposed mechanism linking oxide-induced embrittlement to catastrophic failure must be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: The effect of non-equilibrium processing of SLM is also a great amount of residual stresses, a dense dislocation network, impurities and fine precipitation phases at boundaries []. This defective state was considered in this work as responsible for both the mechanical properties and microstructure evolution during high-temperature aging. Specifically, we reported on the tetragonal σ phase formation in FCC CoCrFeMnNi after thermomechanical processing comprising a room temperature thickness reduction of 90% and subsequent prolonged annealing. Prolonged annealing times were used because of the sluggish diffusion effect that slows down phase transformation. In addition, cold working was used to accelerate phase precipitation [,].

Whereas up to a certain working temperature fine precipitates can play a reinforcing role, starting from a temperature of about 950 K, the σ phase tends to swell and to preferentially place itself on the grain boundaries of the alloy. This in turn can lead to a significant reduction of the mechanical and chemical properties. This is described in the following and confirmed by a mechanical characterization with microhardness and hardness measurements that correlate with the microstructural evolution that occurs during aging.

reading.lever: Modulate the gas atmosphere (oxidizing vs reducing) at elevated temperatures to elucidate precipitate evolution and intergranular oxidation impacts on mechanical failure.
reading.why: This combined approach builds on prior high-temperature mechanical tests and corrosion studies, and it directly tests whether gas-induced surface precipitation governs degradation and catastrophic failure in the target HEA.
